tasks.hint: `flow record LAN-REC`, then `match ipv4 source address`, `match ipv4 destination address`, `match ipv4 protocol`, `collect counter bytes long`, `collect counter packets long`.

tasks.title: Export to the collector
tasks.text: Create exporter `COLLECTOR` sending to `192.168.2.50` on UDP port **2055**, sourced from Gi0/0.
tasks.hint: `flow exporter COLLECTOR`, `destination 192.168.2.50`, `source g0/0`, `transport udp 2055`.

tasks.title: Monitor the LAN and catch a flow
tasks.text: Create monitor `LAN-MON` using that record and exporter, apply it to traffic **entering** Gi0/1, then ping the collector from PC1. The flow should show up in the cache.
tasks.hint: `flow monitor LAN-MON`, `record LAN-REC`, `exporter COLLECTOR`; `interface g0/1`, `ip flow monitor LAN-MON input`. Then `ping 192.168.2.50` on PC1 and `show flow monitor LAN-MON cache` on R1.

title: EEM: an applet that undoes a shutdown
summary: Buffer the logs, write an EEM applet triggered by a syslog pattern that re-enables the WAN link, and test it.
intro:
The **Embedded Event Manager** runs small scripts on the router itself. An **applet** has one `event` (what triggers it) and numbered `action`s (what it does).

- `event syslog pattern "REGEX"` fires when a log message matches the regular expression.
- `action 1.0 cli command "enable"` runs a command as if typed. An applet starts at user EXEC, so `enable` usually comes first.
- `action ... syslog msg "text"` writes its own `%HA_EM-6-LOG` message.

Actions run in the order of their **labels compared as text**, not as numbers: `10.0` runs before `2.0`. Use labels like `1.0`, `2.0` ... `9.0`, or zero-pad them.

Your job: if someone shuts R1's WAN interface Gi0/0, the router should bring it straight back up and say so in the log.

tasks.title: Keep the logs in RAM
tasks.text: Buffer log messages on R1: 8192 bytes, **informational** and above.
tasks.hint: `logging buffered 8192 informational`. `show logging` shows the buffer.

tasks.title: Write the applet
tasks.text: Create applet `NOSHUT-G0` triggered by the message for Gi0/0 going administratively down. It should re-enable Gi0/0 and then log `G0/0 was shut down and has been re-enabled`.
tasks.hint: `event manager applet NOSHUT-G0`; `event syslog pattern "Interface GigabitEthernet0/0, changed state to administratively down"`; actions `1.0` enable, `2.0` configure terminal, `3.0` interface GigabitEthernet0/0, `4.0` no shutdown, `5.0` `syslog msg "..."`.

checks.match: ^ event syslog pattern "Interface GigabitEthernet0/0, changed state to administratively down"$

tasks.title: Test it
tasks.text: Shut Gi0/0. The applet should bring it back, R1 should still reach `2.2.2.2`, and its message should be in the buffer.
tasks.hint: `interface g0/0`, `shutdown`. Then `show ip interface brief`, `show event manager history events` and `show logging`.

checks.pattern: %HA_EM-6-LOG: NOSHUT-G0: G0/0 was shut down and has been re-enabled

R1: event syslog pattern "Interface GigabitEthernet0/0, changed state to administratively down"
action 5.0 syslog msg "G0/0 was shut down and has been re-enabled"

title: Ticket: management services are broken
summary: Five faults on R2: NTP won't sync, nobody can log in, syslog goes nowhere, the NMS is refused over SNMP and LLDP sees no neighbour.
intro:
**Ticket #4471:** *"Since the change window on R2: its clock is wrong, the NOC can't telnet in, our syslog server gets nothing from it, the NMS polls time out and the topology map lost the link to R1."*

The NOC's NMS and syslog server is `NMS` at `192.168.1.100`. R1 is the NTP master (stratum 4, key 1 = `TimeKey`). The NOC logs in as `admin` / `N0cAccess!`.

Work like you would on a real device: `show ntp associations`, `show running-config | section aaa|line vty`, `show logging`, `show access-lists`, `show snmp community`, `show lldp neighbors`. Each task is one fault; fix the cause, don't work around it.

tasks.title: The clock
tasks.text: R2 should synchronise to R1 (`10.12.0.1`) at stratum 5.
tasks.hint: `show ntp associations` shows R1 reachable but not selected. Compare the key *value* on both routers: `show running-config | include ntp` shows them encrypted, so re-enter R2's key 1 as `TimeKey`.

tasks.title: Nobody can log in
tasks.text: `admin` must be able to telnet to R2 and land at privileged EXEC.
tasks.hint: `show running-config | section line vty` against `| include aaa authentication`: the line points at a list that doesn't exist. IOS warned when it was configured.

tasks.title: Syslog goes nowhere
tasks.text: R2's logs must reach the syslog server. Bounce R2's Loopback0 afterwards to prove it.
tasks.hint: `show logging`: the configured host isn't the NMS. Replace it with `logging host 192.168.1.100` (and remove the wrong one).

tasks.title: SNMP polls time out
tasks.text: The NMS must be able to read R2 with community `N3tR3ad`. Keep the community's ACL; fix what it permits.
tasks.hint: `show access-lists 20`: it permits the wrong subnet. The NMS lives in `192.168.1.0/24`.

tasks.title: The topology map
tasks.text: The NMS builds its map from LLDP. R1 should see R2 as a neighbour on Gi0/0.
tasks.hint: `show lldp` on R2.

title: MST: one region, two instances
summary: Replace PVST+ with MST, build a region three switches agree on, and give each instance its own root so both uplinks carry traffic.
intro:
PVST+ runs a spanning tree for **every** VLAN. With hundreds of VLANs that is hundreds of trees to compute and send BPDUs for. **MST** (802.1s) maps many VLANs onto a few **instances**, each with its own tree.

Switches only act as one MST **region** when three things match exactly: the region **name**, the **revision** number and the **VLAN-to-instance table**. One typo and a switch becomes its own region, and the links to it turn into region **boundary** ports that follow instance 0 (the CIST) for every VLAN.

The goal here is load sharing: instance 1 (VLANs 10 and 20) rooted at DSW1, instance 2 (VLANs 30 and 40) rooted at DSW2, so ASW1 sends each half of its VLANs up a different uplink.

| Switch | Links |
|---|---|
| DSW1 | Gi0/1 to DSW2, Gi0/2 to ASW1 |
| DSW2 | Gi0/1 to DSW1, Gi0/2 to ASW1 |
| ASW1 | Gi0/1 to DSW1, Gi0/2 to DSW2, PC1 (VLAN 10) on Fa0/1, PC3 (VLAN 30) on Fa0/3 |

The trunks and VLANs 10, 20, 30 and 40 are already in place. MST uses the long path-cost method, so a gigabit link costs 20000. `show spanning-tree mst` and `show spanning-tree mst configuration` are your friends.

tasks.title: Run MST everywhere
tasks.text: Switch all three switches to MST mode.
tasks.hint: `spanning-tree mode mst` in global configuration on each switch. Until they share a region each switch is a region of one.

tasks.title: Build the region
tasks.text: Configure region **CAMPUS**, revision **1**: instance 1 carries VLANs 10 and 20, instance 2 carries VLANs 30 and 40. All three switches must end up in the same region.
tasks.hint: `spanning-tree mst configuration`, then `name CAMPUS`, `revision 1`, `instance 1 vlan 10,20`, `instance 2 vlan 30,40`, `exit`. The changes apply when you leave the submode. Compare `show spanning-tree mst configuration` on each switch: every field has to match.

tasks.title: A root per instance
tasks.text: Make DSW1 the root for instance 1 and DSW2 the root for instance 2. Each should also be the backup root for the other instance.
tasks.hint: `spanning-tree mst 1 root primary` and `spanning-tree mst 2 root secondary` on DSW1; the opposite on DSW2. Priorities are per instance.

tasks.title: Both uplinks in use
tasks.text: On ASW1 the uplink to DSW1 should forward instance 1 while the uplink to DSW2 forwards instance 2, and the PCs reach their partners in each VLAN.
tasks.hint: `show spanning-tree mst 1` and `show spanning-tree mst 2` on ASW1: the root port changes with the instance and the other uplink is the alternate.

title: Protecting spanning tree
summary: Root guard against a rogue switch, PortFast and BPDU guard on edge ports, loop guard against a one-way BPDU path, and automatic errdisable recovery.
intro:
Spanning tree trusts every BPDU it hears. The protection features decide which ports may be trusted with what:

- **Root guard** on a port that must never lead to the root. A superior BPDU there puts the port in **root-inconsistent** (blocking) instead of moving the root.
- **BPDU guard** on an edge (PortFast) port. Any BPDU err-disables the port.
- **Loop guard** on a root or alternate port. If BPDUs stop arriving, the port goes **loop-inconsistent** instead of becoming designated and opening a loop.
- **errdisable recovery** brings err-disabled ports back after a timer.

DSW1 is meant to be the root (priority 4096). Somebody has plugged a switch called ROGUE, priority 0, into ASW1 Fa0/24, and it has just become the root of the whole network. On top of that, DSW2's downlink to ASW1 has `spanning-tree bpdufilter enable` on it, so ASW1's blocked uplink no longer hears BPDUs and has started forwarding.

Use `show spanning-tree vlan 1` and `show spanning-tree inconsistentports` as you go.

tasks.title: Keep the root where it belongs
tasks.text: Stop ROGUE from being the root bridge without unplugging it. DSW1 must be the root for VLAN 1 again.
tasks.hint: On ASW1, `interface f0/24` and `spanning-tree guard root`. The port goes BKN with `*ROOT_Inc` and the rest of the network forgets the rogue's BPDUs.

tasks.title: Edge port for PC1
tasks.text: Make Fa0/1 on ASW1 a PortFast edge port with BPDU guard, so a switch plugged in there is shut down at once.
tasks.hint: `interface f0/1`, `spanning-tree portfast` and `spanning-tree bpduguard enable`.

tasks.title: Loop guard on the uplinks
tasks.text: Turn on loop guard on both of ASW1's uplinks. The uplink to DSW2 hears no BPDUs, so it should go loop-inconsistent instead of forwarding.
tasks.hint: `interface range g0/1 - 2`, `spanning-tree guard loop`. Then `show spanning-tree vlan 1` on ASW1 shows Gi0/2 as `BKN*` with `*LOOP_Inc`.

tasks.title: Fix the cause
tasks.text: Remove the BPDU filter from DSW2's downlink. ASW1's Gi0/2 should go back to a normal alternate port, blocking.
tasks.hint: `interface g0/2` on DSW2, `no spanning-tree bpdufilter`. BPDU filter on a switch-facing port is almost always a mistake.

tasks.title: Recover by itself
tasks.text: Have ASW1 bring BPDU-guard err-disabled ports back automatically after 60 seconds.
tasks.hint: `errdisable recovery cause bpduguard` and `errdisable recovery interval 60`. `show errdisable recovery` lists the timers.

title: VTP without the disasters
summary: A VTP domain with a server, clients and a password, the configuration revision that can wipe every VLAN, joining a switch safely, and pruning.
intro:
VTP copies the VLAN database from switch to switch over trunks. Within a **domain** (same name and password), the database with the highest **configuration revision** wins and overwrites everyone else's, whatever it contains. A **server** can change VLANs, a **client** only learns them, and a **transparent** switch keeps its own VLANs but passes adverts along.

That is how a lab switch with an old, higher revision can delete every VLAN in production the moment its trunk comes up. The revision goes back to 0 when a switch moves to transparent mode, or when its domain name changes.

SW1 will be the server. SW2 and SW3 should be clients (SW3 is still in transparent mode from its old job). The switch called NEW comes from another building: it is already in domain `CCNP` with password `cisco123`, has a pile of VLANs and a high revision. Its Gi0/1 to SW3 is shut for now.

| Switch | Gi0/1 | Gi0/2 | Access ports |
|---|---|---|---|
| SW1 | SW2 | | PC1 on Fa0/1 (VLAN 10) |
| SW2 | SW1 | SW3 | |
| SW3 | SW2 | NEW | PC2 on Fa0/1 (VLAN 10) |

tasks.title: Set up the domain
tasks.text: On SW1: VTP domain **CCNP**, password **cisco123**, version **2**, server mode.
tasks.hint: `vtp domain CCNP`, `vtp password cisco123`, `vtp version 2`. Server is the default mode. `show vtp status` and `show vtp password` confirm it.

tasks.title: Clients learn the VLANs
tasks.text: Make SW2 and SW3 VTP clients in the same domain. SW3 should learn VLAN 10 (USERS), and PC1 and PC2 can then ping.
tasks.hint: `vtp mode client` and `vtp password cisco123` on each. A client with no domain name takes the domain from the first advert it hears. SW3's Fa0/1 is in VLAN 10, which only exists there once VTP brings it.

tasks.title: Join NEW without wiping the domain
tasks.text: Bring NEW's Gi0/1 up as a VTP client of the domain. SW1 must keep its VLANs, and NEW must end up with VLAN 10.
tasks.hint: Compare `show vtp status` on NEW and SW1: NEW's revision is higher. Put NEW in transparent mode first (that resets the revision to 0), then `vtp mode client`, and only then `no shutdown` on Gi0/1. If you bring it up first, its database replaces SW1's and you'll have to rebuild the VLANs.

tasks.title: Prune what nobody uses
tasks.text: Turn on VTP pruning so VLAN 20 isn't flooded down trunks to switches that have no ports in it.
tasks.hint: `vtp pruning` on the server; the clients learn it. `show interfaces trunk` on SW1: VLAN 20 drops out of the last section, "Vlans in spanning tree forwarding state and not pruned".

title: VRRPv3: an open-standard gateway
summary: VRRPv3 between two routers: the address-family syntax, master election, tracking the uplink and a real failover test.
intro:
**VRRP** does the job of HSRP but is an IETF standard, so it works between different vendors. The differences that trip people up:

- The roles are **master** and **backup** (not active and standby).
- **Preemption is on by default.**
- A router whose real interface address *is* the virtual IP is the **owner** and always wins with priority 255.
- The virtual MAC is `0000.5e00.01xx`, where xx is the group number in hex.

Newer IOS uses **VRRPv3** with its own syntax: `fhrp version vrrp v3` once globally, then a group per interface with `vrrp <group> address-family ipv4`, and `address`, `priority`, `track` inside it.

R1 and R2 both reach CORE, which has `8.8.8.8` on a loopback. The PCs already point at `192.168.10.1`, which nobody owns yet. Track 1 on R1 follows its uplink Gi0/1.

| Router | LAN Gi0/0 | Uplink Gi0/1 |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | 192.168.10.2 | 10.1.0.1 |
| R2 | 192.168.10.3 | 10.2.0.1 |

tasks.title: VRRPv3 group 10
tasks.text: Enable VRRPv3 on both routers and create group 10 on Gi0/0 with virtual address `192.168.10.1`. R1 gets priority 120 and should be the master.
tasks.hint: `fhrp version vrrp v3`, then `interface g0/0`, `vrrp 10 address-family ipv4`, `address 192.168.10.1 primary`, `priority 120` (R1 only), `exit-vrrp`. `show vrrp brief` shows MASTER and BACKUP.

tasks.title: The PCs use it
tasks.text: Both PCs should reach `8.8.8.8` through the virtual gateway.
tasks.hint: From PC1, `ping 8.8.8.8`, then `show arp`: the gateway's MAC is `00:00:5e:00:01:0a`, the VRRP virtual MAC for group 10.

tasks.title: Track the uplink
tasks.text: If R1's uplink fails, R1 should give up the master role: lower its priority by 30 when track 1 goes down.
tasks.hint: Inside `vrrp 10 address-family ipv4` on R1: `track 1 decrement 30`. 120 - 30 = 90, below R2's 100.

tasks.title: Prove the failover
tasks.text: Shut R1's Gi0/1, check that R2 becomes the master and the PCs still reach 8.8.8.8, then bring Gi0/1 back. R1 should take over again on its own.
tasks.hint: `interface g0/1`, `shutdown` on R1, `show vrrp brief` on R2, a ping from a PC, then `no shutdown`. Preemption (on by default) lets R1 back in.

title: GLBP: share the gateway
summary: One virtual IP, two routers forwarding at once: the AVG hands each host a different virtual MAC, weighting decides who forwards, and forwarders survive their router.
intro:
HSRP and VRRP leave the standby router idle. **GLBP** (Cisco) lets every router in the group forward.

- One router is the **AVG** (active virtual gateway, highest priority, then highest IP). It answers every ARP for the virtual IP.
- Each router is an **AVF** (active virtual forwarder) with its own virtual MAC, `0007.b400.xxyy` (group xx, forwarder yy).
- The AVG hands out those MACs in turn (**round-robin**, the default), or by **weighting**, or by **host-dependent** hashing.
- **Weighting** with thresholds decides whether a router still forwards. If its weighting falls below the lower threshold, another AVF takes over its MAC.

Only R1 needs to be told the virtual IP: `glbp 1 ip` on its own lets R2 learn it from the AVG.

The PCs point at `192.168.10.1`. CORE has `8.8.8.8`. Track 1 on R1 follows its uplink.

| Router | LAN Gi0/0 | Uplink Gi0/1 |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | 192.168.10.2 | 10.1.0.1 |
| R2 | 192.168.10.3 | 10.2.0.1 |

tasks.title: Group 1 with R1 as AVG
tasks.text: Configure GLBP group 1 on both routers' Gi0/0 with virtual IP `192.168.10.1`. R1 gets priority 150 and preempt, so it is the AVG.
tasks.hint: R1: `glbp 1 ip 192.168.10.1`, `glbp 1 priority 150`, `glbp 1 preempt`. R2: `glbp 1 ip` (it learns the address). `show glbp brief` lists the AVG and both forwarders.

tasks.title: Both routers forward
tasks.text: Ping `8.8.8.8` from all three PCs. The AVG should hand them out across both routers' virtual MACs.
tasks.hint: Compare `show arp` on the PCs: different PCs get `00:07:b4:00:01:01` and `00:07:b4:00:01:02`. Round-robin goes to the next forwarder with each new host.

tasks.title: Weight the uplink
tasks.text: On R1, set weighting 100 with a lower threshold of 70 and an upper threshold of 90, and drop it by 40 when track 1 goes down.
tasks.hint: `glbp 1 weighting 100 lower 70 upper 90` and `glbp 1 weighting track 1 decrement 40`. With the uplink down R1 falls to 60, below 70, and stops forwarding.

tasks.title: Lose R1's uplink
tasks.text: Shut R1's Gi0/1: R2 should take over R1's forwarder (forwarding both virtual MACs) and every PC still reaches 8.8.8.8. Then bring the uplink back.
tasks.hint: `shutdown` on R1 Gi0/1, `show glbp brief` on R2 (both forwarders Active), a ping from each PC, then `no shutdown`. R1 is still the AVG throughout: only forwarding moved.

title: SPAN and RSPAN: copy the traffic
summary: A local SPAN session to an IDS, a remote-span VLAN across a trunk, and an RSPAN session that delivers copies to an analyzer on another switch.
intro:
**SPAN** copies the frames crossing source ports or VLANs to a destination port where a sniffer or IDS listens. A destination port stops being a normal switch port: it doesn't forward ordinary traffic and shows as **monitoring**.

**RSPAN** sends the copies across the network in a dedicated VLAN marked `remote-span` on every switch it crosses. The source switch's session ends in `destination remote vlan`, the far switch's session starts with `source remote vlan`. (**ERSPAN** does the same over IP with GRE, configured on routers.)

PC1 and PC2 share VLAN 10 on SW1. IDS sits on SW1 Fa0/24, ANALYZER on SW2 Fa0/24. The SW1-SW2 link is a trunk already. Pings generate the traffic: send a few after each session.

tasks.title: Mirror PC1 to the IDS
tasks.text: On SW1, session 1 copies everything PC1's port sends and receives to Fa0/24. Then ping PC2 from PC1 so the IDS gets copies.
tasks.hint: `monitor session 1 source interface f0/1 both` and `monitor session 1 destination interface f0/24`. `show monitor session 1` and `show interfaces status` (Fa0/24 shows monitoring).

tasks.title: An RSPAN VLAN
tasks.text: Create VLAN 900 as a remote-span VLAN on both switches.
tasks.hint: `vlan 900`, `remote-span`. `show vlan remote-span` lists it. Without the attribute, a switch learns MAC addresses in that VLAN and the copies go nowhere useful.

tasks.title: Copies to the analyzer
tasks.text: Session 2 on SW1 sends everything received in VLAN 10 into RSPAN VLAN 900; session 1 on SW2 takes VLAN 900 to Fa0/24. Ping again so the analyzer gets copies.
tasks.hint: SW1: `monitor session 2 source vlan 10 rx` and `monitor session 2 destination remote vlan 900`. SW2: `monitor session 1 source remote vlan 900` and `monitor session 1 destination interface f0/24`.

SW1: monitor session 1 source interface f0/1 both

title: DHCP snooping, DAI and IP source guard
summary: Block a rogue DHCP server with snooping, get past the option-82 trap, then use the binding table for dynamic ARP inspection and IP source guard.
intro:
Three features that build on each other:

1. **DHCP snooping** splits ports into **trusted** (towards real servers) and **untrusted**. Server messages (offers, acks) arriving on an untrusted port are dropped, so a rogue server can't hand out addresses. It also records a **binding**: MAC, IP, VLAN and port for each lease.
2. **Dynamic ARP inspection** checks every ARP on untrusted ports against those bindings (or an ARP ACL), so nobody can claim someone else's IP.
3. **IP source guard** drops IP packets whose source address isn't the one bound to that port.

One classic trap: snooping inserts **DHCP option 82** with a zero relay address. An IOS DHCP server drops such requests unless it trusts the relay information (`ip dhcp relay information trust-all`), or the switch stops inserting it (`no ip dhcp snooping information option`).

R1 (Gi0/1 uplink) is the real DHCP server for 10.1.1.0/24, handing out .100 and up. ROGUE on Fa0/24 runs its own DHCP server. PC1 and PC2 use DHCP. SERVER has the static address 10.1.1.50.

tasks.title: Snoop and trust the uplink
tasks.text: Turn on DHCP snooping for VLAN 1 on SW1 and trust only the uplink to R1.
tasks.hint: `ip dhcp snooping`, `ip dhcp snooping vlan 1`, and on `interface g0/1`, `ip dhcp snooping trust`. Every other port stays untrusted, including the rogue's.

tasks.title: A real lease for PC1
tasks.text: PC1 should get its address from R1 (10.1.1.100 or above), not from ROGUE, and SW1 should have a binding for it.
tasks.hint: Try `ip dhcp` on PC1. If nothing answers, it's option 82: either `ip dhcp relay information trust-all` on R1 or `no ip dhcp snooping information option` on SW1. Then `show ip dhcp snooping binding`.

tasks.title: Inspect ARP
tasks.text: Turn on dynamic ARP inspection for VLAN 1. PC1 must still reach R1, and so must SERVER, whose static address has no binding.
tasks.hint: `ip arp inspection vlan 1`. The router's ARP replies arrive on the uplink, so trust it: `ip arp inspection trust` on Gi0/1. For SERVER (its MAC is in `show ip` on SERVER), an ARP ACL: `arp access-list STATIC`, `permit ip host 10.1.1.50 mac host 0050.7966.6805`, then `ip arp inspection filter STATIC vlan 1`.

tasks.title: Lock PC2's source address
tasks.text: Give PC2 a lease, then turn on IP source guard on its port. PC2 can only use the address it was given.
tasks.hint: `ip dhcp` on PC2, then `interface f0/2`, `ip verify source`. `show ip verify source` lists the address allowed on the port.

SW1: no ip dhcp snooping information option
ip arp inspection filter STATIC vlan 1

title: Private VLANs
summary: Split one subnet with private VLANs: isolated hosts that only reach the gateway, a community that can talk among itself, and a promiscuous router port.
intro:
A **private VLAN** splits one VLAN (and one subnet) into pieces that can't talk to each other at layer 2, while everyone keeps the same gateway:

- The **primary** VLAN is the whole thing. A **promiscuous** port (the router) belongs to it and talks to everyone.
- An **isolated** secondary VLAN: its hosts reach only promiscuous ports, not each other.
- A **community** secondary VLAN: its hosts reach each other and the promiscuous ports, but not other communities or isolated hosts.

With VTP versions 1 and 2, private VLANs can only be configured in **transparent** mode.

Plan: primary VLAN 100, isolated VLAN 101 for the hotel rooms ROOM1 and ROOM2, community VLAN 102 for the staff PCs STAFF1 and STAFF2. R1 on Gi0/1 is the gateway, 10.1.0.1. The PCs are addressed and currently all sit in VLAN 1, so they can all reach each other.

tasks.title: The private VLANs
tasks.text: Put SW1 in VTP transparent mode, then create primary VLAN 100 associated with isolated VLAN 101 and community VLAN 102.
tasks.hint: `vtp mode transparent`, `vlan 101` + `private-vlan isolated`, `vlan 102` + `private-vlan community`, `vlan 100` + `private-vlan primary` + `private-vlan association 101,102`. `show vlan private-vlan`.

tasks.title: Host ports
tasks.text: The rooms go in isolated VLAN 101, the staff PCs in community VLAN 102.
tasks.hint: `interface range f0/1 - 2`, `switchport mode private-vlan host`, `switchport private-vlan host-association 100 101`; the same for f0/3 - 4 with 102.

tasks.title: A promiscuous gateway
tasks.text: Make Gi0/1 (to R1) a promiscuous port mapped to both secondary VLANs. Every PC reaches 10.1.0.1.
tasks.hint: `interface g0/1`, `switchport mode private-vlan promiscuous`, `switchport private-vlan mapping 100 101,102`.

tasks.title: Check the isolation
tasks.text: Confirm it: the rooms can't reach each other or the staff, but the staff PCs reach each other.
tasks.hint: Ping from ROOM1 to ROOM2 and STAFF1 (both fail), and from STAFF1 to STAFF2 (works). Same subnet, different layer-2 reach.

title: Layer-3 switching
summary: Route between VLANs on the switch itself: ip routing, SVIs as gateways, a routed uplink with a default route, a voice VLAN and protected kiosk ports.
intro:
A multilayer switch can route between VLANs in hardware, with no router-on-a-stick. Three pieces:

- `ip routing` turns routing on. Without it the switch is a layer-2 switch with a management address.
- An **SVI** (`interface vlan 10`) is the gateway for each VLAN. It comes up while some port in the VLAN is up.
- `no switchport` makes a physical port a **routed port**, with its own IP address, like a router interface.

Two access-layer extras live here too. A **voice VLAN** puts an IP phone's traffic in its own tagged VLAN while the PC behind it stays untagged in the access VLAN. **Protected ports** on the same switch can't talk to each other, only to unprotected ports.

| VLAN | Subnet | Gateway (SVI) | Ports |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 Users | 10.1.10.0/24 | .1 | PC1 on Fa0/1 |
| 20 Servers | 10.1.20.0/24 | .1 | SRV1 on Fa0/2 |
| 30 Kiosks | 10.1.30.0/24 | .1 | KIOSK1, KIOSK2 on Fa0/3, Fa0/4 |

The VLANs, access ports and SVIs are configured. The uplink Gi0/1 to ISP should be 10.0.0.1/30; ISP is 10.0.0.2 and has `8.8.8.8`.

tasks.title: Route between the VLANs
tasks.text: Turn on routing so PC1 reaches SRV1 through the SVIs.
tasks.hint: `ip routing`. `show ip route` lists the SVI subnets as connected. Before that, `show ip route` only prints the default gateway.

tasks.title: A routed uplink
tasks.text: Make Gi0/1 a routed port with 10.0.0.1/30 and send everything else to ISP with a default route. PC1 should reach 8.8.8.8.
tasks.hint: `interface g0/1`, `no switchport`, `ip address 10.0.0.1 255.255.255.252`, `no shutdown`, then `ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.0.0.2`. `show interfaces status` lists Gi0/1 as routed.

tasks.title: A phone on PC1's port
tasks.text: An IP phone is going in front of PC1. Give Fa0/1 voice VLAN 150 (create VLAN 150 named VOICE first).
tasks.hint: `vlan 150`, `name VOICE`, then `interface f0/1`, `switchport voice vlan 150`. `show interfaces f0/1 switchport` shows the voice VLAN; the phone's frames are tagged 150, PC1's stay untagged in VLAN 10.

tasks.title: Kiosks keep to themselves
tasks.text: The two kiosks must not reach each other, though both still reach their gateway.
tasks.hint: `interface range f0/3 - 4`, `switchport protected`. Protected ports don't forward to each other on the same switch.

title: Ticket: the campus after the change window
summary: Four faults left by last night's change: a broken MST region, a VTP domain typo, two VRRP masters and DHCP snooping that blocks every lease.
intro:
Last night's change window went badly and the morning's tickets are in:

> *"PC1 gets no address."* *"PC2 can't reach the file server PC3."* *"show vrrp says both routers are master."* *"The new access switch shows boundary ports in show spanning-tree mst."*

Find and fix each fault without redesigning anything. The intended design:

- DSW1 and ASW1 form one MST region: name **CAMPUS**, revision **1**, instance 1 = VLANs 10 and 20.
- VTP domain **CAMPUS**: DSW1 is the server, ASW1 a client.
- R1 and R2 run **VRRP group 10** on Gi0/0 with virtual IP 10.10.10.254. R1 (priority 110) is master.
- R1 is the DHCP server for VLAN 10. ASW1 runs DHCP snooping on VLAN 10 and does not insert option 82.

| Device | Notes |
|---|---|
| DSW1 | Gi0/1 R1, Gi0/2 R2, Fa0/23 trunk to ASW1, PC3 (VLAN 20) on Fa0/1 |
| ASW1 | Fa0/23 trunk to DSW1, PC1 (VLAN 10, DHCP) on Fa0/1, PC2 (VLAN 20) on Fa0/2 |

ASW1: no ip dhcp snooping information option

tasks.title: One MST region
tasks.text: ASW1 must be in the same MST region as DSW1.
tasks.hint: `show spanning-tree mst configuration` on both: compare name, revision and the instance table. Fix ASW1 to match the design.

tasks.title: VLAN 20 across the switches
tasks.text: PC2 reaches the file server PC3 in VLAN 20.
tasks.hint: `show vtp status` on ASW1: look closely at the domain name. A client in the wrong domain learns nothing, so VLANs 10 and 20 don't exist on ASW1 and its ports in them are inactive.

tasks.title: One master
tasks.text: R1 is master for VRRP group 10 and R2 is its backup.
tasks.hint: `show vrrp brief` on both. The routers must agree on the group number to hear each other. Fix R2: `no vrrp 11`, `vrrp 10 ip 10.10.10.254`.

tasks.title: PC1 gets an address
tasks.text: PC1 gets a lease from R1 and reaches its gateway, 10.10.10.254.
tasks.hint: With VLAN 10 now on ASW1, try `ip dhcp` on PC1 and look at ASW1's console: offers are dropped on an untrusted port. Trust the uplink: `ip dhcp snooping trust` on Fa0/23.

title: Multi-area OSPF: ABRs and area summaries
summary: Split the network into areas 0, 1 and 2, watch ABRs turn intra-area routes into summary LSAs, and summarise area 1 at its border.
intro:
A single OSPF area floods every router LSA to every router and reruns SPF everywhere when anything changes. **Areas** contain that: routers only hold the full topology of their own area, and **area border routers (ABRs)** describe everything else with **type-3 summary LSAs**, which show up as `O IA` routes.

R1 already runs area 1 and R3 the backbone. Finish the design on R2 and R4, then summarise area 1 so the backbone carries one route for R1's three LANs instead of three.

| Link | Network | Area |
|---|---|---|
| R1 - R2 | 10.0.12.0/24 | 1 |
| R2 - R3 | 10.0.23.0/24 | 0 |
| R3 - R4 | 10.0.34.0/24 | 0 |
| R1 LAN + loopbacks | 172.16.0.0/24, 172.16.1.0/24, 172.16.2.0/24 | 1 |
| R4 LAN | 192.168.4.0/24 | 2 |

Useful: `show ip ospf`, `show ip ospf database`, `show ip ospf border-routers`, `show ip route ospf`.

tasks.title: Make R2 the area 1 ABR
tasks.text: Put R2's link to R1 in **area 1** and its link to R3 in **area 0**. `show ip ospf` on R2 should say *It is an area border router*.
tasks.hint: `router ospf 1`, then `network 10.0.12.0 0.0.0.255 area 1` and `network 10.0.23.0 0.0.0.255 area 0`.

tasks.title: Add area 2 at R4
tasks.text: R4's uplink is in the backbone and its LAN (`192.168.4.0/24`) is **area 2**. Keep hellos off the LAN.
tasks.hint: `network 10.0.34.0 0.0.0.255 area 0`, `network 192.168.4.0 0.0.0.255 area 2` and `passive-interface g0/2`.

tasks.title: Summarise area 1
tasks.text: On the ABR, advertise R1's three `172.16.x.0/24` networks into the backbone as one **172.16.0.0/22**. R2 installs a discard route for the range.
tasks.hint: `area 1 range 172.16.0.0 255.255.252.0` under `router ospf 1` on R2. Then `show ip route 172.16.0.0` on R2 shows the Null0 route.

tasks.title: End to end
tasks.text: PC1 should reach PC4 across all three areas.
tasks.hint: If it fails, check `show ip route` on each router for the other side's LAN.

title: OSPF stub, totally stubby and NSSA areas
summary: Shrink a branch's routing table with stub and totally stubby areas, then let another branch import partner routes as an NSSA.
intro:
Branch routers rarely need every route. A **stub** area keeps out external (type-5) LSAs and gets a default route from its ABR instead; **totally stubby** (`no-summary` on the ABR) also drops the inter-area summaries. Neither may contain an ASBR.

A **not-so-stubby area (NSSA)** is the exception: it blocks type-5 LSAs but may hold its own ASBR, whose routes travel as **type-7** LSAs (`O N2`) and are translated to type 5 (`O E2`) by the ABR.

Here R1 originates a default (`O*E2`), R3 is a branch in area 1, and R5 in area 2 imports two partner networks with `redistribute static` - which only works while area 2 allows externals.

Every router in an area must agree on the area type, or the adjacency drops (*Mismatched Stub/Transit area option bit*).

tasks.title: Make area 1 a stub
tasks.text: Configure area 1 as a **stub** on both R2 and R3. R3 then gets `O*IA` default from R2 and loses R1's `O*E2` default.
tasks.hint: `area 1 stub` under `router ospf 1` on both routers. Configure one side and watch the adjacency drop until the other matches.

tasks.title: Make it totally stubby
tasks.text: Keep the inter-area routes out too, so R3's table has its own routes and one default.
tasks.hint: Only the ABR needs it: `area 1 stub no-summary` on R2.

tasks.title: Bring in the partner routes
tasks.text: R5 must redistribute its two static routes (`192.168.50.0/24` and `.51.0/24`) into OSPF. Make **area 2 an NSSA** so it may, then redistribute.
tasks.hint: `area 2 nssa` on R4 and R5, then on R5 `redistribute static subnets`. R4 sees `O N2`, R1 sees `O E2` (R4 translated them).

tasks.title: Give the NSSA a default
tasks.text: An NSSA gets no default route automatically. Have R4 inject one into area 2.
tasks.hint: `area 2 nssa default-information-originate` on R4. R5 then shows `O*N2 0.0.0.0/0`.

title: OSPF virtual links and MD5 authentication
summary: Unstick an adjacency stuck in EXSTART, join a discontiguous area to the backbone with a virtual link, and secure the backbone with MD5.
intro:
Every area must touch area 0. Area 2 here hangs off area 1 instead, so R3 can't summarise it into the backbone and R4 can't reach anything. A **virtual link** through transit area 1 gives R3 a logical backbone connection: both ends name each other's router ID (`area 1 virtual-link <rid>`).

First, though, R1 and R2 never get past **EXSTART**: their interface MTUs differ, so the router with the smaller MTU rejects the other's database descriptions. Fix the MTU (or tell OSPF to ignore it).

Finally, protect the R1-R2 link with **MD5** (`ip ospf authentication message-digest` plus a matching `ip ospf message-digest-key`). `debug ip ospf adj` shows exactly why a mismatched key fails.

tasks.title: Fix the stuck adjacency
tasks.text: R1 and R2 sit in EXSTART. Find out why and bring them to FULL.
tasks.hint: `show ip ospf neighbor` shows EXSTART; compare `show ip interface g0/0` on both. Remove `ip mtu 1400` on R2 (or add `ip ospf mtu-ignore` on R2, the side with the smaller MTU).

tasks.title: Join area 2 to the backbone
tasks.text: Build a virtual link between R2 (2.2.2.2) and R3 (3.3.3.3) through area 1.
tasks.hint: `area 1 virtual-link 3.3.3.3` on R2 and `area 1 virtual-link 2.2.2.2` on R3. `show ip ospf virtual-links` says *up*.

tasks.title: Authenticate the R1-R2 link
tasks.text: Use MD5 with key ID 1 and the key `NetLab1` on both ends. The adjacency must come back to FULL.
tasks.hint: On each g0/0: `ip ospf authentication message-digest` and `ip ospf message-digest-key 1 md5 NetLab1`.

title: EIGRP stub routing, summarisation and authentication
summary: Summarise a branch's networks, stop branches acting as transit with eigrp stub, and secure the WAN links with key-chain MD5.
intro:
The hub reaches two branches, and the branches also have a slow backup link to each other. Three problems:

1. S1's three LANs reach the hub as three routes. An **interface summary** (`ip summary-address eigrp`) on S1's uplink sends one `172.16.0.0/22` instead and installs a **Null0** discard route on S1.
2. Without help, the hub can reach S2 *through* S1 over the slow link. **`eigrp stub`** makes a branch advertise only its own routes, so it is never used as transit (and is never queried).
3. The WAN needs **MD5** authentication: a `key chain` plus `ip authentication mode eigrp 100 md5` and `ip authentication key-chain eigrp 100 <chain>` on each end.

`show ip eigrp neighbors detail` shows stub peers; `show ip eigrp topology` shows the summary.

tasks.title: Summarise S1's LANs
tasks.text: Send the hub a single **172.16.0.0/22** for S1's three networks.
tasks.hint: On S1: `interface g0/0` then `ip summary-address eigrp 100 172.16.0.0 255.255.252.0`.

tasks.title: Make the branches stubs
tasks.text: Configure both spokes as EIGRP stubs (the default: connected and summary routes).
tasks.hint: `router eigrp 100` then `eigrp stub` on S1 and S2. The hub's `show ip eigrp neighbors detail` lists *Stub Peer Advertising ( CONNECTED SUMMARY ) Routes*.

tasks.title: Authenticate the WAN
tasks.text: Create key chain **WAN** with key 1 and key-string **NetLab1** on all three routers, and use MD5 on the hub-spoke links (`g0/0` and `g0/1` on the hub, `g0/0` on each spoke).
tasks.hint: `key chain WAN` / `key 1` / `key-string NetLab1`, then on each interface `ip authentication mode eigrp 100 md5` and `ip authentication key-chain eigrp 100 WAN`.

tasks.title: End to end
tasks.text: PC2 should reach S1's LAN 172.16.2.1, and S2 should hold the hub's summary for it.
tasks.hint: Check `show ip route eigrp` on S2: the /22 comes from the hub; the /24s still arrive over the backup link, and the longer match wins.

title: Named-mode EIGRP for IPv4 and IPv6
summary: Run one named EIGRP instance with an IPv4 and an IPv6 address family, wide metrics and per-interface settings in af-interface.
intro:
Named mode puts everything EIGRP does under one `router eigrp <name>`: an **address family** per protocol (`address-family ipv4 unicast autonomous-system 10`, `address-family ipv6 unicast autonomous-system 10`), interface settings in **`af-interface`**, and redistribution and variance in **`topology base`**. It also uses 64-bit **wide metrics**.

The IPv6 family needs no `network` statements: every IPv6-enabled interface joins unless you shut it in `af-interface`. Neighbours talk over link-local addresses, and the router ID still comes from IPv4 (each router has a loopback).

The PCs already have IPv4 addresses and take IPv6 addresses by SLAAC.

tasks.title: IPv4 address family
tasks.text: On all three routers, start `router eigrp NETLAB` with the IPv4 family in AS **10**, covering `10.0.0.0/8` and each LAN.
tasks.hint: `router eigrp NETLAB`, `address-family ipv4 unicast autonomous-system 10`, `network 10.0.0.0`, `network 192.168.1.0` (R1) / `192.168.3.0` (R3).

tasks.title: IPv6 address family
tasks.text: Add the IPv6 family (also AS 10) to the same named instance on all three routers.
tasks.hint: Under `router eigrp NETLAB`: `address-family ipv6 unicast autonomous-system 10`. Check `show ipv6 eigrp neighbors`.

tasks.title: Quiet the LANs
tasks.text: Make the PC-facing interfaces passive in both families on R1 and R3.
tasks.hint: In each family: `af-interface g0/2` then `passive-interface`.

title: Mutual redistribution between RIP and OSPF
summary: Redistribute in both directions at two points, then fix the suboptimal path it causes and tag routes so they never loop back.
intro:
R1 runs RIP; R4 runs OSPF; R2 and R3 sit on the boundary and run both. Redistribution needs a **seed metric** into RIP (otherwise the routes are unreachable, metric 16), and `subnets` into OSPF.

With two redistribution points a classic problem appears: R3 learns R1's networks by RIP (AD **120**) and also as `O E2` from R2 (AD **110**). OSPF wins, so R3 sends traffic for R1 the long way round. Raising OSPF's external distance above 120 on the boundary routers fixes it.

**Route tags** are the standard loop guard: tag RIP routes as they enter OSPF, and refuse tagged routes on the way back into RIP.

tasks.title: RIP into OSPF
tasks.text: On **both** R2 and R3, redistribute RIP into OSPF, tagging the routes **120** with a route-map called `RIP-TO-OSPF`.
tasks.hint: `route-map RIP-TO-OSPF permit 10` / `set tag 120`, then under `router ospf 1`: `redistribute rip subnets route-map RIP-TO-OSPF`.

tasks.title: OSPF into RIP, without the loop
tasks.text: Redistribute OSPF into RIP on both boundary routers with a seed metric of **3**, through a route-map `OSPF-TO-RIP` that **denies tag 120** and permits the rest.
tasks.hint: `route-map OSPF-TO-RIP deny 10` / `match tag 120`, `route-map OSPF-TO-RIP permit 20`, then `redistribute ospf 1 metric 3 route-map OSPF-TO-RIP` under `router rip`.

tasks.title: Fix the long way round
tasks.text: R3 now reaches R1's networks through OSPF via R4 and R2. Make the boundary routers prefer RIP for them by raising OSPF's **external** distance to **125** on R2 and R3.
tasks.hint: `distance ospf external 125` under `router ospf 1`. Then `show ip route 172.16.1.0` on R3 is a RIP route via 10.1.13.1.

title: Route filtering with prefix-lists, distribute-lists and offset-lists
summary: Keep a lab network out of the core with a prefix-list and distribute-list, then steer traffic onto the better path with an offset-list.
intro:
The branch BR advertises its user LAN, a server LAN and a lab network that must never reach the core. It has two equal uplinks, through A and through B.

**Prefix-lists** match prefixes *and* lengths (`ge`/`le`), and a list ends with an implicit deny. A **distribute-list** applies one to the routes a protocol accepts (`in`) or sends (`out`). An **offset-list** adds to the metric of matching routes, which is the gentle way to prefer one of two equal EIGRP paths.

`show ip prefix-list detail` shows hit counts as routes are checked.

tasks.title: Keep the lab network out
tasks.text: On CORE, build prefix-list **NO-LAB** that denies exactly `192.168.99.0/24` and permits everything else, and apply it to the routes EIGRP accepts.
tasks.hint: `ip prefix-list NO-LAB seq 5 deny 192.168.99.0/24`, `ip prefix-list NO-LAB seq 10 permit 0.0.0.0/0 le 32`, then `distribute-list prefix NO-LAB in` under `router eigrp 1`.

tasks.title: Prefer path A for users
tasks.text: CORE load-shares to 192.168.10.0/24 over A and B. Make it use **only A** for that network by adding 1000 to its metric on routes learned from B.
tasks.hint: `access-list 10 permit 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255`, then under `router eigrp 1`: `offset-list 10 in 1000 g0/1`.

CORE: ip prefix-list NO-LAB seq 10 permit 0.0.0.0/0 le 32

title: IP SLA tracking and policy-based routing
summary: Make the default route follow a live probe of ISP1, fall back to ISP2, and send guest traffic out ISP2 with PBR.
intro:
EDGE has two ISPs. A static default to ISP1 stays installed even when ISP1's router dies, because the link to it can stay up. **IP SLA** fixes that: an `icmp-echo` probe runs every few seconds, a **track** object follows its reachability, and `ip route ... track 1` withdraws the route the moment the probe fails. A **floating static** (higher distance) via ISP2 takes over.

**Policy-based routing** overrides the routing table per packet: a route-map matched against an ACL sets the next hop, and `ip policy route-map` on the *incoming* interface applies it. Here the guest LAN should always leave by ISP2.

`show ip sla statistics`, `show track` and `show route-map` (policy match counts) show it working; `debug ip policy` prints each decision.

tasks.title: Probe ISP1
tasks.text: Create IP SLA **1**: an ICMP echo to ISP1 (`10.1.0.2`) sourced from g0/0 every 5 seconds, running forever. Track its reachability as object **1**.
tasks.hint: `ip sla 1` / `icmp-echo 10.1.0.2 source-interface g0/0` / `frequency 5`, then `ip sla schedule 1 life forever start-time now` and `track 1 ip sla 1 reachability`.

tasks.title: A tracked default with a backup
tasks.text: Default to ISP1 tied to track 1, and a floating default to ISP2 with distance **10**.
tasks.hint: `ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.1.0.2 track 1` and `ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.2.0.2 10`. Shut ISP1's g0/0 to watch the backup take over, then bring it back.

tasks.title: Send guests out ISP2
tasks.text: Guest traffic (`192.168.20.0/24`) must always leave by ISP2, whatever the routing table says. Use ACL **120** and route-map **GUEST**.
tasks.hint: `access-list 120 permit ip 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 any`, `route-map GUEST permit 10` / `match ip address 120` / `set ip next-hop 10.2.0.2`, then `ip policy route-map GUEST` on g0/3.

EDGE: ip sla schedule 1 life forever start-time now

title: DHCPv6 relay and IPv6 ACLs
summary: Hand out IPv6 addresses from a remote DHCPv6 server through a relay, then filter the client LAN without breaking neighbour discovery.
intro:
CL is a router acting as an IPv6 host (no `ipv6 unicast-routing`): it takes its address by **stateful DHCPv6** (`ipv6 address dhcp`) and its default route from router advertisements. The server SV is two hops away, so RL must **relay** (`ipv6 dhcp relay destination`) and set the **managed** flag in its RAs.

IPv6 ACLs (`ipv6 access-list`, applied with `ipv6 traffic-filter`) end with three implicit lines: permit ND neighbour advertisements, permit ND neighbour solicitations, then deny everything. An *explicit* `deny ipv6 any any` at the end comes **before** those implicit permits, so neighbour discovery fails and nothing works - unless you permit `nd-na` and `nd-ns` first.

tasks.title: Serve addresses from SV
tasks.text: On SV create DHCPv6 pool **LAN** handing out `2001:db8:10::/64` with DNS server `2001:db8::53`, and serve it on g0/0.
tasks.hint: `ipv6 dhcp pool LAN` / `address prefix 2001:db8:10::/64` / `dns-server 2001:db8::53`, then `ipv6 dhcp server LAN` on SV's g0/0.

tasks.title: Relay for the client LAN
tasks.text: On RL's g0/0, set the managed-config flag and relay DHCPv6 to SV (`2001:db8:23::3`). CL should get an address and reach SV.
tasks.hint: `ipv6 nd managed-config-flag` and `ipv6 dhcp relay destination 2001:db8:23::3` on RL g0/0. `show ipv6 dhcp interface` on CL shows the lease.

tasks.title: Filter the client LAN
tasks.text: Inbound on RL g0/0, allow only ICMP echo requests from `2001:db8:10::/64` to SV, and deny everything else **with a logged** `deny ipv6 any any log`. CL must still reach SV, and must not reach RL's `2001:db8:23::2`.
tasks.hint: `ipv6 access-list CLIENT-IN` with `permit icmp any any nd-na`, `permit icmp any any nd-ns`, `permit icmp 2001:db8:10::/64 host 2001:db8:23::3 echo-request`, `deny ipv6 any any log`; then `ipv6 traffic-filter CLIENT-IN in` on g0/0.

title: ENARSI troubleshooting ticket: OSPF and EIGRP
summary: A four-fault ticket: authentication, an MTU mismatch and two redistribution mistakes stand between PC1 and PC4.
intro:
**Ticket #4471:** *"Users on PC1 (`192.168.1.0/24`) can't reach the server LAN behind R4 (`192.168.4.0/24`). Nothing was changed. Honestly."*

R1, R2 and R3 run OSPF area 0; R3 and R4 run EIGRP 100, and R3 redistributes between them. Work like the exam: confirm the symptom, follow the path, and fix each fault where it is, without redesigning anything.

Good tools: `show ip ospf neighbor`, `debug ip ospf adj`, `show ip ospf interface`, `show ip interface`, `show ip protocols`, `show ip route`, `show ip eigrp topology`, `show run | section router`.

tasks.title: Fault 1: R1 and R2
tasks.text: R1 and R2 aren't OSPF neighbours. Fix it on R1.
tasks.hint: `debug ip ospf adj` on R2 shows *Mismatched Authentication Key - Message Digest Key 1*. Look closely at R1's key (zero vs O).

tasks.title: Fault 2: R2 and R3
tasks.text: R2 and R3 are neighbours but stuck. Fix it without changing R3.
tasks.hint: `show ip ospf neighbor` on R3 shows EXSTART. Compare MTUs with `show ip interface`; R2's g0/1 has `ip mtu 1400`.

tasks.title: Fault 3: OSPF into EIGRP
tasks.text: R4 has no route to 192.168.1.0/24 even though R3 has it. Fix the redistribution on R3 with a seed metric of `10000 100 255 1 1500`.
tasks.hint: Redistributing into EIGRP without a metric gives nothing. `redistribute ospf 1 metric 10000 100 255 1 1500` under `router eigrp 100`.

tasks.title: Fault 4: EIGRP into OSPF
tasks.text: R1 learns nothing from the EIGRP side. Fix the redistribution on R3 so every subnet is carried.
tasks.hint: Without `subnets`, OSPF only takes classful networks. `redistribute eigrp 100 subnets`.

title: Multicast: PIM sparse mode with a static RP
summary: Turn on multicast routing and PIM sparse mode, point every router at a rendezvous point, join a group from a PC and watch the shared tree turn into a source tree.
intro:
Unicast routing sends a packet **to** someone. Multicast routing sends one stream **toward everyone who asked for it**, and the routers build the delivery tree backwards, from the receivers toward the source.

- **IGMP** is how a host tells its router *I want group 239.1.1.1*. It runs on any interface with PIM enabled.
- **PIM sparse mode** builds a **shared tree** first: the last-hop router sends a `(*,G)` join hop by hop toward the **rendezvous point (RP)**. The source's first-hop router *registers* its packets to the RP, which sends them down the shared tree.
- After the first packet the last-hop router joins the **source tree** `(S,G)` directly toward the source (the *SPT switchover*). Every join follows the **RPF** interface: the one the router would use to reach the RP or source in its unicast table.

R1's Loopback1 (10.1.1.1) stands in for the video server, R2's Loopback0 (2.2.2.2) will be the RP, and PC3 is the viewer. OSPF already runs everywhere.

| Device | Address | Role |
|---|---|---|
| R1 Loopback1 | 10.1.1.1/24 | Source (first-hop router) |
| R2 Loopback0 | 2.2.2.2/32 | Rendezvous point |
| R3 G0/1 | 10.1.3.3/24 | Receivers' LAN (last-hop router) |
| PC3 / PC4 | 10.1.3.10 / 10.1.3.11 | PC3 joins the group; PC4 doesn't |

VPCS has no IGMP, so NetLab adds one command to the PCs: `mcast join GROUP` (and `mcast leave GROUP`).

Useful: `show ip pim neighbor`, `show ip pim rp mapping`, `show ip igmp groups`, `show ip mroute`, `show ip rpf`.

tasks.title: Turn on multicast routing
tasks.text: Enable multicast forwarding on **R1, R2 and R3**. Until then a router runs neither PIM nor multicast forwarding.
tasks.hint: Global configuration: `ip multicast-routing` (IOS XE wants `ip multicast-routing distributed`).

tasks.title: Run PIM sparse mode
tasks.text: Enable `ip pim sparse-mode` on every router-to-router link and on R3's LAN (G0/1), so IGMP runs there too. `show ip pim neighbor` on R2 should list both R1 and R3.
tasks.hint: On R1: G0/0. On R2: G0/0 and G0/1. On R3: G0/0 and G0/1. `interface range g0/0 - 1` saves typing.

tasks.title: Point everyone at the RP
tasks.text: Sparse mode needs a rendezvous point. Make **2.2.2.2** the RP for all groups, statically, on all three routers. `show ip pim rp mapping` should show it as *Static*.
tasks.hint: `ip pim rp-address 2.2.2.2` on R1, R2 and R3. Every router must agree on the RP.

tasks.title: Join the group from PC3
tasks.text: On PC3 run `mcast join 239.1.1.1`. R3 hears the IGMP report, and as the LAN's DR sends a `(*,G)` join toward the RP. Look at `show ip igmp groups` and `show ip mroute 239.1.1.1` on R3, then on R2.
tasks.hint: R3's `(*, 239.1.1.1)` should have flags **SJC** and G0/1 in its outgoing list; R2's entry should forward out G0/1 toward R3.

tasks.title: Stream to the group
tasks.text: From R1 run `ping 239.1.1.1 repeat 3 source loopback1`. PC3 replies; PC4 never joined, so it doesn't. Then compare `show ip mroute 239.1.1.1` on R1 and R3: R1 has an `(S,G)` with the **F** (register) flag, and R3 has switched to the source tree (**T**).
tasks.hint: `source` comes last on IOS's ping line. If nobody replies, check `show ip pim rp mapping` on R1 and `show ip mroute` on R2.

title: Multicast: Auto-RP finds the RP for you
summary: Replace hand-typed RP addresses with Auto-RP: a candidate RP announces itself, a mapping agent picks the RP and tells every router.
intro:
A static RP works until you have fifty routers and need to move it. **Auto-RP** (Cisco) automates the mapping:

1. A **candidate RP** sends *RP announcements* to group **224.0.1.39**.
2. A **mapping agent** listens to 224.0.1.39, picks the RP for each group range (the highest address wins) and sends *RP discovery* messages to **224.0.1.40**.
3. Every router listens to 224.0.1.40 and learns *group range → RP*.

The catch: those two groups are flooded in **dense mode**, and nobody knows the RP for them yet. On interfaces that run pure sparse mode they go nowhere, unless you add `ip pim autorp listener` (or run `sparse-dense-mode`).

Multicast routing and PIM sparse mode already run on every link here, and PC3 has joined 239.2.2.2, but no router knows an RP, so the group goes nowhere. Make **R2 (2.2.2.2)** the candidate RP and **R3 (3.3.3.3)** the mapping agent.

Useful: `show ip pim rp mapping`, `show ip mroute`, `show ip pim rp`.

tasks.title: Let Auto-RP cross sparse-mode links
tasks.text: Auto-RP's own groups (224.0.1.39 and 224.0.1.40) need dense-mode flooding. Allow it on **R1, R2 and R3** without changing the interfaces' PIM mode.
tasks.hint: `ip pim autorp listener` in global configuration on all three routers.

tasks.title: Announce R2 as a candidate RP
tasks.text: Have R2 announce its Loopback0 as a candidate RP for all groups, with a TTL scope of 16 hops.
tasks.hint: On R2: `ip pim send-rp-announce loopback0 scope 16`.

tasks.title: Make R3 the mapping agent
tasks.text: Have R3 send RP discovery messages from its Loopback0 (scope 16). Every router should then learn 2.2.2.2 as the RP, *elected via Auto-RP*, in `show ip pim rp mapping`.
tasks.hint: On R3: `ip pim send-rp-discovery loopback0 scope 16`. R3 must hear R2's announcements first, which is why task 1 matters.

tasks.title: Stream to the group
tasks.text: R3 can now join the shared tree toward the RP it learned. From R1 run `ping 239.2.2.2 source loopback1` and get PC3's reply.
tasks.hint: `show ip mroute 239.2.2.2` on R3 shows RP 2.2.2.2 and flags **SJC** once the mapping is in place.

title: Ticket: the multicast stream never arrives
summary: Three faults stand between the source and the viewer: IGMP isn't running, an RPF check fails, and one router has the wrong RP.
intro:
> **Ticket #4471** — *The training video on 239.10.10.10 plays fine in the head office but the branch (PC3) sees nothing. PC3 has definitely joined the group.*

R1's Loopback1 (10.1.1.1) is the source, R2's Loopback0 (2.2.2.2) is the RP, PC3 sits behind R3. The R1–R3 link is a cheap backup circuit that only carries unicast: OSPF prefers it, so the R2–R3 link has a higher cost, and that must stay that way.

| Link | Network | PIM? |
|---|---|---|
| R1 – R2 | 10.1.12.0/24 | yes |
| R2 – R3 | 10.1.23.0/24 | yes (OSPF cost 100) |
| R1 – R3 | 10.1.13.0/24 | no (unicast only) |
| R3 LAN | 10.1.3.0/24 | — |

Work from the receiver toward the source. Useful: `show ip igmp interface`, `show ip igmp groups`, `show ip rpf`, `show ip pim neighbor`, `show ip pim rp mapping`, `show ip mroute`.

tasks.title: R3 never hears PC3's join
tasks.text: PC3 has joined 239.10.10.10, yet `show ip igmp groups` on R3 is empty. Make R3 learn the membership on G0/1.
tasks.hint: IGMP runs on interfaces where PIM runs. `show ip igmp interface g0/1` on R3 says *IGMP is disabled on interface*.

tasks.title: R3's join can't reach the RP
tasks.text: Now R3 has a `(*,G)` entry, but the RP (R2) never sees the join. Compare `show ip rpf 2.2.2.2` with `show ip pim neighbor` on R3. Fix it **without** changing unicast routing: R3 must keep reaching 2.2.2.2 through R1.
tasks.hint: R3's RPF interface toward the RP is G0/2, which doesn't run PIM, so the join is never sent. A static mroute (`ip mroute 2.2.2.2 255.255.255.255 10.1.23.2`) overrides the RPF interface for multicast only. Running PIM on the R1–R3 link also works.

tasks.title: The source's router has the wrong RP
tasks.text: R1 is the source's first-hop router, so it registers the stream to the RP. Make R1 agree with everyone else on the RP.
tasks.hint: `show ip pim rp mapping` on R1 shows 2.2.2.22. Remove it and configure `ip pim rp-address 2.2.2.2`.

tasks.title: The stream reaches the branch
tasks.text: From R1 run `ping 239.10.10.10 source loopback1`. PC3 should reply.
tasks.hint: If nothing comes back, walk the path again: IGMP on R3, the (*,G) on R2, and the RP mapping on R1.

title: Sandbox
summary: Two routers, two switches, four PCs, blank configs. Build whatever you like.
intro:
No tasks and no checks: a blank network to practise on. The routers are cabled to each other and each has a switch with two PCs.

Some ideas: put R1 and R2 on `10.0.12.0/30` and run OSPF between them; give each LAN its own VLANs with router-on-a-stick; lock both routers down with SSH and an ACL. **Reset** wipes everything back to blank.

SW1 and SW2 are also joined by two cables (Fa0/23 and Fa0/24), so you can try spanning tree and EtherChannel.
